title: CPCB Says Diwali Data Gaps Came From Older Monitors' 1,000-Microgram Ceiling
excerpt: In an 11-point clarification issued Tuesday, the Central Pollution Control Board said hourly readings above the calibrated range of its older particulate analysers were automatically treated as errors and dropped from Delhi's averages — and rejected allegations of under-reporting.
body:
• The CPCB said on Tuesday that the particulate analysers deployed when India's air quality index was introduced in 2015 were calibrated to measure 0–1,000 micrograms per cubic metre — and its automated validation system treats any hourly reading beyond that range as an error.
  • Those excluded hours do not count toward a station's 24-hour average, which the board said "may appear as a data gap" during extreme episodes such as the Diwali firecracker burst.
  • The board defended the AQI ceiling of 500 as a design feature of the index: above 500, the reading stays in the 'Severe' category and the health risk is much the same, it said.
  • The CPCB said the methodology is under review, including how to process readings beyond the designed range, and that older instruments are being replaced; Delhi's monitoring stations have grown from 10 to 59.

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has explained, in its first detailed response, why Delhi's official pollution record went blank at station after station during the peak of Diwali night: the instruments and the validation rules behind them were built with a ceiling of 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre, and anything above it was discarded as an error. In an 11-point statement posted on X on Tuesday, November 10, the board rejected allegations of under-reporting and said the data gaps, and the wide differences with private air-quality apps, were attributable to differences in measurement and methodology, ANI reported.

"The difference in AQI values is thus attributable to differences in measurement of pollutant concentration and in methodology, and not to under-reporting."

— Central Pollution Control Board

How the peak hours vanished

The mechanism is built into the system that has run since the National Air Quality Index (NAQI) was introduced in 2015. The particulate matter analysers deployed at that time were calibrated for a measurement range of 0–1,000 micrograms per cubic metre. The automated data validation system therefore treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range, and such readings are not used in the computation of a station's AQI. "During extreme episodes, which are occasional like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of relevant pollutant for concerned station," the board said.

What that meant on Diwali night, according to the reporting that prompted the clarification, is that the missing hours were the most polluted ones. A Hindustan Times analysis of data later released by the Delhi Pollution Control Committee found 125 station-hour readings that were missing from the CPCB record and that all of them exceeded 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre; the highest, at Mundka, reached 3,744 micrograms per cubic metre at 2 a.m. on November 9. At 1 a.m. that night, 36 of Delhi's 59 stations had no PM2.5 reading in the CPCB's records.

Why the apps showed four-digit numbers

The board also addressed the second controversy: screenshots of private apps showing Delhi AQI readings of 1,500 to over 2,000 while the official index reported values under 400. The NAQI, developed by the CPCB through IIT Kanpur and launched in 2015, is built to reflect sustained exposure: it uses the average of the preceding 24 hours for most pollutants (eight hours for carbon monoxide and ozone), and the index itself runs from 0 to 500, with 500 representing the highest level of health concern. Private platforms, the board said, use data from government and non-government sources including low-cost sensors with calibration limitations, calculate AQI from instantaneous hourly readings, and apply different breakpoints. Such apps can therefore show higher values during short peaks — and lower values than the NAQI once concentrations fall, because the official index continues to reflect the previous 24 hours of exposure.

What changes now

The board acknowledged that monitoring technology has advanced since 2015. It said the replacement of older instruments and the expansion of the monitoring network are being undertaken continuously — continuous ambient air quality monitoring stations have grown from 30 across India in 2014-15 to 634 at present, and in Delhi from 10 to 59. The methodology itself is kept under review, and the board said internal deliberations and consultations are under way on how to process data beyond the system's designed measurement range. It advised citizens to follow the health advisories attached to the prevailing AQI category, particularly for children, the elderly and people with respiratory or cardiac conditions.

What the explanation does not settle

The clarification establishes why the hours are missing; it does not restore them. The excluded readings were the highest of the night, so Delhi's published Diwali averages rest on a record from which the peak was systematically removed — the point critics, including the Centre for Science and Environment's Anumita Roychowdhury, had pressed when the gaps were first reported. Whether the review now under way changes how above-range readings are handled before the next extreme episode is the outcome to watch.
